lead: A phone, a washing machine and a car's brake controller all run on ARM cores. ARM is a RISC design built on three rules: every instruction is 32 bits long, only load and store instructions touch memory, and the ALU works on registers. Those rules let the core pipeline fetch, decode and execute without guessing where the next instruction starts. This chapter covers the RISC idea, ARM's data-flow model, the family tree from ARM7 to Cortex-M, the meaning of the letters in ARM7TDMI, and byte order.
prereq: You need: CISC and RISC design philosophy, von Neumann and Harvard memory, and pipelining basics from Unit 1, Foundations.

sections.h3: RISC against CISC, and ARM's rules

blocks.text: CISC and RISC are two deals about instruction complexity. A CISC machine keeps many instruction lengths, lets an arithmetic instruction read its operand straight from memory, and uses a microcode layer to crack each instruction into small internal steps. A RISC machine keeps a small set of simple instructions, all the same length, and expects most of them to finish in one clock.
ARM follows the RISC deal with four concrete rules:

items: Fixed 32-bit instructions. Every ARM instruction is exactly 4 bytes and sits on a word boundary (address divisible by 4).
Load-store data path. ADD, SUB, AND, MOV and friends work only on registers. Memory is reached through LDR (load register) and STR (store register).
Many registers. Sixteen registers R0-R15 are visible at once, so the compiler spills to memory less often.
Condition codes. Almost every instruction can test the flags and skip itself, which removes many short branches.

blocks.text: Why bother? A fixed length means the decoder knows where each instruction begins before the fetch finishes, so stages can overlap safely. Keeping memory out of the ALU path means the arithmetic never waits on a slow memory read. These two choices are what make a clean pipeline possible.
You meet this everywhere: a Chennai-made UPI card reader, a fitness band, a bike's engine control unit. Each one wants small code, low current and predictable timing.

sections.h3: The data-flow model and the 3-stage pipeline

blocks.text: Picture the core as a register file feeding an ALU, with memory sitting off to one side behind a narrow door. Data-processing instructions read one or two source registers, produce a result and write it to a destination register. Only LDR moves a word from memory into a register, and only STR moves a word from a register into memory.

items: Fetch. The core reads the 32-bit instruction from the address held in the program counter.
Decode. The control unit works out the operation, the source registers and the destination register.
Execute. The register file sends operands to the ALU, the ALU computes, and the result is written back in the same clock.

For LDR or STR, the address is computed in the execute stage and the data transfer finishes in that same cycle for zero-wait-state memory; a slow memory simply stretches the execute cycle by extra clocks.

blocks.where: T is the total time in seconds to run N instructions on a pipeline of k stages, and t_clk is one clock period in seconds. For the classic 3-stage ARM pipeline k = 3.

blocks.text: The 3-stage pipeline is the reason R15 reads strangely. While an instruction executes, two later instructions are already fetched, so reading R15 gives the address of the current instruction plus 8 in ARM state. This offset is a pipeline effect, not a design mistake.

sections.h3: Families, and the letters in ARM7TDMI

blocks.text: ARM licenses cores; it does not make most of the chips. The cores split into two eras.

head: Family
Role
rows: 5-stage pipeline, separate instruction and data paths
application profile: phones and tablets that run an operating system
real-time profile: hard deadlines such as disk drives and engine control

blocks.text: The name ARM7TDMI is a list of features. T = Thumb, a 16-bit encoding of common instructions. D = debug, on-chip support for breakpoints. M = enhanced multiplier, a 32 × 32 bit multiply producing a 64-bit result. I = embedded ICE, an on-chip debug unit reached through a JTAG port. Read the letters as a shopping list, not as one word.
ARM7TDMI itself is a von Neumann core: one 32-bit bus carries both instructions and data. Do not assume every ARM chip is Harvard. Check the specific core and the memory system around it.

A 32-bit word occupies four byte addresses. Which byte goes first is the endianness. In little-endian, the least significant byte sits at the lowest address. In big-endian, the most significant byte sits there.

Most ARM cores support both byte orders, and the memory system selects one; a few small Cortex-M cores are little-endian only, so check the specific core. Most real boards run little-endian. Take the word 0x12345678 stored at address 0x4000. Little-endian gives 78 56 34 12 at 0x4000 to 0x4003. Big-endian gives 12 34 56 78. The same number, two byte layouts. Network protocols often use big-endian, which is why most ARM cores can switch.

figure.caption: ARM's classic 32-bit cores grew into three Cortex profiles. Notice ARM7's three pipeline stages against ARM9's five, and the three Cortex letters A, R, M.

spec.aria: ARM family tree: Classic ARM7, ARM9 and ARM11 sit beside Cortex-A, Cortex-R and Cortex-M under the ARM root.

examples.question: An ARM7TDMI system uses little-endian memory. The 32-bit word 0x12345678 is stored starting at address 0x4000. (a) List the four bytes at 0x4000 to 0x4003 in hex and in decimal. (b) Show that reading the four bytes back rebuilds the original word. (c) State what the letters T, D, M and I mean in ARM7TDMI. (8 marks)
steps: Little-endian rule: the least significant byte of the word goes to the lowest address.
Split 0x12345678 into bytes, most significant first: 0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78.
The least significant byte is 0x78, so address 0x4000 gets 0x78 = 120 in decimal.
Read back: 0x12 × 2²⁴ + 0x34 × 2¹⁶ + 0x56 × 2⁸ + 0x78 = 0x12345678 = 305419896 in decimal, the original word.
Suffix: T = Thumb 16-bit encoding, D = debug support, M = enhanced multiplier, I = embedded ICE on-chip debug.
examples.answer: The bytes at 0x4000 to 0x4003 are 78, 56, 34, 12 in hex (120, 86, 52, 18 in decimal); read back they rebuild 0x12345678 = 305419896, and the suffix letters mean Thumb, debug, multiplier and embedded ICE.
examples.check:
w = 0x12345678
base = 0x4000
b = [(w >> (8*i)) & 0xFF for i in range(4)]
for x in b:
    print(x)
read_back = b[0] | (b[1] << 8) | (b[2] << 16) | (b[3] << 24)
print(read_back)

examples.question: A 3-stage ARM pipeline runs 100 instructions at a clock period of 20 ns. How long does the whole sequence take? (4 marks)
steps: Use T = (N + k − 1) × t_clk with N = 100 instructions, k = 3 stages, t_clk = 20 ns.
The first instruction takes 3 clocks to fill the pipeline; the remaining 99 instructions retire one per clock, so 3 + 99 = 102 clocks.
examples.answer: The 100 instructions take 2040 ns, that is 2.04 µs.

traps: Saying every ARM core is bi-endian. Most support both byte orders and the memory system selects one, but a few small Cortex-M cores are little-endian only, so check the specific core.
Calling ARM7TDMI Harvard. It is a von Neumann core with one bus. Deeper cores such as ARM9 have separate instruction and data paths.
Writing ADD R1, R2, [R3] as if ARM allowed a memory operand. ARM is load-store: you must LDR first, add, then STR.
Mixing the suffix letters. D is debug, not DSP; M is the enhanced multiplier, not memory.
Forgetting the pipeline offset. In ARM state, reading R15 gives the current instruction address plus 8, not plus 0.

quiz.q: What does the T in ARM7TDMI stand for, and what does it give the programmer?
quiz.a: T stands for Thumb: a set of 16-bit encodings of common ARM instructions. Code becomes smaller; the CPU stays the same and can switch between ARM and Thumb state.

quiz.q: Why does a fixed 32-bit instruction length make pipelining easier than a variable length?
quiz.a: With every instruction 4 bytes long and word-aligned, the fetch stage knows the next address before the current instruction is decoded. Stages can advance together every clock without stalling to find instruction boundaries. Variable lengths force the decoder to finish before the next fetch address is known.

quiz.q: A little-endian ARM stores the word 0x0A0B0C0D at address 0x2000. Give the byte at each address 0x2000 to 0x2003 in hex.
quiz.a: Least significant byte 0x0D goes to 0x2000, then 0x0C at 0x2001, 0x0B at 0x2002, 0x0A at 0x2003. Order: 0D 0C 0B 0A.

quiz.q: A 3-stage ARM pipeline runs 50 instructions at a clock period of 10 ns with no stalls. Find the total time.
An anti-lock brake controller needs a guaranteed response within microseconds. Which Cortex profile fits, and why not Cortex-A?
quiz.a: Cortex-R. It is built for real-time, deterministic response to interrupts and has tightly coupled memory. Cortex-A targets applications with an operating system, caches and memory management, so worst-case response time cannot be guaranteed.

quiz.q: ARM arithmetic instructions cannot read from memory. Give one cost and one benefit of that rule.
quiz.a: Cost: one memory-based operation becomes three instructions (LDR, ADD, STR), so code size grows. Benefit: every data-processing instruction finishes in one clock because operands come from registers, never from memory, so the pipeline stays simple and the clock can be fast. It also keeps every operand in a register, so a register-to-register operation has fixed, predictable timing.

quiz.q: Why is a 32-bit word stored in a different byte order on big-endian and little-endian machines, while the number itself is unchanged?
quiz.a: Endianness is only a convention about which byte address holds which part of the word. The bit pattern of the 32-bit value is identical; only the four byte addresses are assigned in reverse order.

beyond: Not for the exam. ARM moved past 32-bit with ARMv8-A and its AArch64 state, which has 31 general registers and fixed 32-bit instructions again. Cortex-M cores now ship with Helium (M-vector extension) for small DSP work, and the open RISC-V instruction set borrows heavily from the same load-store philosophy. To go further, search for AArch64 registers, Cortex-M55, and the M-profile exception model. Reading a real datasheet next to this chapter will make the pipeline offset and endianness settings concrete.
